abstract: Optical skyrmions are topological forms of structured light offering an unbounded encoding alphabet robust to perturbations. However, their practical use is limited by the absence of a topological detector, since states distinguished by their topological invariant, N, are not necessarily orthogonal. Here, we demonstrate the first deterministic detector for optical skyrmions using a deep diffractive neural network trained in real time, with the number of training parameters reduced by a factor of 1000. The network comprises two independent processing channels, each containing five diffractive layers, that map input topologies onto spatially separated output channels, enabling identification of N. We demonstrate the detector using 81 topologies constructed from vectorial Laguerre-Gaussian modes, achieving high accuracy even at noise levels that preclude conventional Stokes polarimetry. Finally, we transmit and recover an image encoded using a 15-level topological alphabet with negligible crosstalk, demonstrating a practical route towards topology-enabled optical communication. The article presents the first direct detector of optical skyrmionic topologies using a deep diffractive neural network, enabling seamless detection of symbols encoded in skyrmionic topology. Its simplified phase layers reduce network complexity and enable in situ training.
title: Deep diffractive optical neural networks for detecting skyrmionic topologies of light and their live training

title: Photonic neuromorphic learning via generalized in situ physical gradient descent

abstract: To improve integrated photonic systems for optical computing applications, the ability to control both the amplitude and phase of microring modulator transmission is a key capability for advanced photonic integrated circuits. In this work, we present a novel dual-gate microring modulator that integrates a Z-shaped silicon PN junction with a graphene overlay, offering enhanced electro-optic tunability beyond conventional single-gate designs. The device consists of two electrically coupled active regions, one PN junction and the other incorporating graphene, allowing modulation of both the real and imaginary parts of the effective refractive index through control voltages V an and V gr . This dual-gate approach provides control over the transmission phase and amplitude, which are important for complex-valued modulation in programmable photonic circuits. We further demonstrate its utility by implementing a simplified optical neural network (ONN) architecture to illustrate end-to-end feasibility, achieving accuracies of 93.4% and 81.95% on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets, respectively. Multiphysics simulations using Lumerical Charge, finite-difference eigenmode (FDE), and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) validate the modulator’s performance and highlight its potential for next-generation integrated photonic computing platforms.
title: Graphene-enhanced dual-gate electro-optic micro-ring modulator: An optical neural network design

abstract: Abstract Optical computing encodes and processes information through the continuous evolution of optical fields, whereas digital electronic systems operate on discrete logical states. Conventional optical-to-electronic interfaces convert measured optical responses into electronically accessible data, with task-specific interpretation subsequently performed in the electronic domain. Here, we introduce and experimentally validate a proof-of-concept light-field-to-bits (LFB) computing architecture that maps information-bearing light fields onto predefined 4-bit codewords. The proposed architecture comprises two cascaded diffractive layers that route optical energy at the output plane into eight predefined regions of interest (ROIs) arranged as four differential pairs, with each pair encoding one bit through relative-intensity comparison. We physically implement the first diffractive layer and computationally emulate the second, using a CMOS sensor to capture the intermediate intensity distribution. We further develop a differentiable physics-assisted surrogate model within a camera-in-the-loop framework. The experimental prototype achieves 4-bit codeword accuracies of 95.31% for geometrically perturbed hexadecimal inputs and 93.36% for traffic-sign inputs subjected to combined viewpoint distortion and noise. Meanwhile, the optical front-end exploits the intrinsic parallelism of diffractive propagation, performing high-dimensional optical transformations equivalent to ∼51.2 Giga-Operations (GOPs) of multiply accumulate (MAC) operations within a ∼1.16 ns optical time-of-flight, while the electronic stage only performs lightweight spatial aggregation at the scale of tens of Mega-FLOPs. This strategy establishes the feasibility of LFB computing as an interface between continuous optical information processing and discrete digital decision-making for latency-sensitive machine vision and edge sensing.
title: Light-Field-to-Bits Computing via an Online-Trainable Cascaded Optoelectronic Neural Network

abstract: Matrix–matrix multiplication (MMM) is the dominant computational primitive in modern deep-learning workloads, and its electronic implementation is increasingly bounded by the energy and interconnect limits of CMOS. Existing photonic accelerators largely perform only matrix–vector multiplication or operate at limited scale. We present a free-space photonic MMM architecture that combines two thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) phase-only spatial light modulators (SLMs) in a 4-f Fourier relay to perform true C=A⋅B in the outer-product, time-integrating regime of Athale and Collins [ Appl. Opt. 21 , 2089 ( 1982 ). APOPAI 0003-6935 10.1364/AO.21.002089 ], replacing kilohertz-rate liquid-crystal or acousto-optic modulation with gigahertz-rate electro-optic phase modulation. The outer product is formed by cascading a row-encoded and a column-encoded amplitude mask in an imaging relay; the Fourier shift theorem is used to place the amplitude-carrying diffraction order of each phase-only SLM in a Fourier-plane spatial filter. We derive the architecture from first principles and validate it with a three-layer physical simulation: scalar-diffraction modeling of the pixelated SLMs and 4-f relay, a full detector-noise Monte Carlo of the time-integrating accumulation, and end-to-end neural-network inference executed entirely through the physical model. Carrier-order placement is accurate to 0.09% of the row pitch with an 8-bit phase DAC; at the nominal 100 mW design point, the simulated processor achieves 6.4 effective bits at N=128 under a conservative 100 ps photon-integration window (about 8 bits when photons are integrated over the full 1 ns cycle), shot-noise limited, and 95.8% classification accuracy on a handwritten-digit benchmark versus 98.3% for float32 and INT8 digital execution. We quantify the effect of inter-pixel phase blur on the phase-only amplitude encoding end-to-end, showing that a two-level checkerboard with a blur of 0.1 pixel pitch limits the usable matrix dimension to N≈64 unless guard rows are added between macropixels, give a full-latency (compute plus readout) throughput and energy accounting, and break down the assumed optical efficiency and the physical volume. For N=1024, the compute subsystem projects 2 PFLOPS at sub-10 fJ/MAC; including detector readout with a pipelined read-out integrated circuit and a deep inner dimension, the full-latency figures are 1.7 PFLOPS at ≈9fJ/MAC, and the simulation quantifies the optical power (≈0.6−6W, depending on the integration window) required to reach INT8 precision at that scale.
title: Gigahertz thin-film lithium niobate phase-SLM architecture for true matrix–matrix multiplication in photonic AI accelerators: design and physical-layer simulation
